lead.kicker: TOP STORY  •  UK AND THE EU
lead.headline: Britain and the EU Strike a Deal That Opens Doors for Young People
lead.deck: About 100,000 young Britons a year could live, work or study in Europe for up to three years.
body: Ten years after 52% of British voters chose to leave the European Union, Britain has agreed to move closer again. On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham met EU leaders in Brussels, where the 27-member bloc has its headquarters, and agreed a package of deals.

For teenagers, the key part is a Youth Experience Scheme. Each year about 100,000 young Britons will be able to spend up to three years in EU countries travelling, working or studying, and about 100,000 young Europeans can do the same in Britain. “Brexit did take away opportunity from young people,” Burnham said. Talks on cutting tuition fees for European students at UK universities are still to come. Under an earlier agreement, the UK is also due to rejoin the Erasmus+ student exchange programme in 2027.

The deal also reaches the shopping basket. From March 2028 the UK will follow EU food standards rules, which ministers say will cut paperwork; Treasury analysis suggests this could add about 0.5% to the UK economy. Britain will also join the EU's carbon market for electricity, and the two sides promised closer cooperation on defence.

Not everyone approves: Oliver Lewis of the Stay Out campaign called it “a humiliating spectacle for the Prime Minister.” Burnham is still bound by Keir Starmer's promise not to rejoin the EU's single market or customs union, and a bill to put the deal into law is due next week.

lead.why: For anyone at secondary school now, this could decide how easy it is to live, work or study in an EU country after school, and it shows Britain rebuilding ties with its neighbours without rejoining.

world.headline: Big Three Leave Ukraine Off Their List, and Berlin Answers Back
world.deck: Trump, Xi and Putin agreed on oil, the UN and nuclear risk. Europe says it will not be carved up again.
body: On Thursday, US President Donald Trump, China's President Xi Jinping and Russia's President Vladimir Putin held their first-ever three-way meeting, at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the APEC summit. They talked for about an hour and a half, then issued a short joint statement. It promised to reform the United Nations, to increase oil and gas production “for the benefit of all countries,” to stop the International Criminal Court abusing its powers, and to avoid nuclear war.

What the statement left out mattered most to Europe. It did not mention Russia's war in Ukraine, now in its fifth year, and neither Ukraine's government nor any European official was in the room. Putin ruled out talks with Ukraine after a Ukrainian strike on the bridge linking Russia to Crimea, and said Ukraine and Europe were “not yet ready” to compromise. Trump, by contrast, rated the meeting a 12 on a scale of 0 to 10.

Europe answered from Berlin on the same day. Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz hosted Ukraine's backers, known as the Coalition of the Willing, including Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky, France's Emmanuel Macron and the UK's Andy Burnham. Merz called Shenzhen a “photo op” and recalled the Yalta Conference of 1945, when, he said, Europe was “parcelled up.” He promised: “we won't allow anything like that to happen again.”

A seat at the table may still be possible. Merz said new peace talks involving Europe, Ukraine, Russia and the US could happen soon, naming the UAE as a possible venue, and Trump's envoy Jared Kushner said Russia had agreed to talks that include Europe. Putin made a different offer: he proposed that European envoys come to Moscow.

illustration.title: THREE LEADERS, ONE TABLE
illustration.subtitle: Shenzhen, 19 November
illustration.caption: The three leaders met for about an hour and a half; neither Ukraine nor any European official was there.

world.connect: Connect the dots: In February 1945, Roosevelt, Churchill and Stalin met at Yalta, and Merz says Europe's future was divided up there. That is why he reached for Yalta this week, and why he handed leaders pieces of the Berlin Wall, which he said brought “oppression, insecurity and a lack of peace.”

uk.headline: Record Diesel Price Pushes UK Inflation Up to 3.6%
uk.deck: Fuel costs climb with the Middle East conflict, while food price rises slow to their gentlest since 2021.
body: Inflation measures how fast prices are rising. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said on Wednesday that prices in October were 3.6% higher than a year earlier, up from 3.5% in September: the fourth monthly rise in a row.

Fuel did most of the pushing. The average litre of diesel rose 7p in a month to 199.5p, the highest since ONS records began in 1996. The rise is linked to the conflict in the Middle East, which has pushed up energy prices around the world.

Food tells a different story: its price rises slowed to 0.9%, the slowest since September 2021. Earlier this month the Bank of England raised interest rates to 4%, and it warns inflation could reach around 5% by the middle of next year.
uk.why: When inflation stays high, the Bank of England may raise interest rates, which changes what families pay on mortgages and earn on savings.
also: Energy bills: a forecast says the typical price cap could rise 26% to about £2,166 in January.
Youth jobs: 981,000 people aged 16 to 24 in England and Wales are out of work, school or training.

europe.headline: Russian Missiles Fall in Poland During a Huge Night Attack on Ukraine
europe.deck: Nobody in Poland was hurt, but its prime minister called it a Russian “provocation.”
body: Overnight into Friday, Russia launched a massive attack on Ukraine. Ukraine's Air Force counted 84 cruise missiles and 404 attack drones, and President Volodymyr Zelensky said 27 ballistic missiles were also fired. At least nine people were killed, and three of Kyiv's bridges were damaged.

Some of the weapons crossed into Poland, a member of both the EU and NATO. A Kh-101 cruise missile came down about 60 km from the Ukrainian border, and another missile and a drone fell elsewhere. Nobody was hurt. Prime Minister Donald Tusk called it a Russian “provocation,” and NATO chief Mark Rutte condemned “grave violations” of Polish airspace.

call.question: Should a country follow its neighbours' food rules to make trade easier?
call.premise: Under the new deal, the UK will follow EU food standards rules from March 2028. Ministers say this will cut paperwork, and Treasury analysis suggests it could add about 0.5% to the UK economy.
call.evidence: From March 2028 the UK will follow EU food standards rules, which ministers say will cut paperwork
call.framing: Hypothetical decision based on this story.

options.label: Follow EU rules
options.benefit: Less paperwork for food trade with the EU, and Treasury analysis suggests the economy could grow by about 0.5%.
options.cost: The UK follows food rules that are written by the EU rather than in Britain.

options.label: Keep UK rules
options.benefit: Britain keeps writing its own food rules and can change them as it chooses.
options.cost: Food trade with the EU keeps its extra paperwork, and the possible economic boost is lost.

lead.headline: Britain and Europe Make a New Deal
body: Ten years ago, most British voters chose to leave the European Union, or EU. The EU is a group of 27 countries that work together.
On Friday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham met EU leaders in Brussels. They agreed a deal to bring Britain and the EU closer again.

Under the deal, about 100,000 young Britons each year can live, work or study in EU countries for up to three years. About 100,000 young Europeans can come to Britain too. Britain will also follow EU rules on food from March 2028. Ministers say that means less paperwork.
Some people do not like the deal. One campaigner called it humiliating for the Prime Minister.

world.headline: Three Big Leaders Meet, but Leave Out Ukraine
body: The leaders of the US, China and Russia met together for the first time. They met in Shenzhen, a city in China, for about an hour and a half.
They agreed to pump more oil and gas and to avoid nuclear war. But they did not mention the war in Ukraine. Nobody from Ukraine or Europe was there.
In Berlin, Germany's leader Friedrich Merz met Ukraine's friends. He said big powers must never again divide Europe up, as he says they did at Yalta in 1945.

uk.headline: Prices Rise Faster in the UK
body: Inflation tells us how fast prices are going up. In October, UK prices were 3.6% higher than a year before.
Fuel was the main reason. A litre of diesel cost 199.5p on average. That is the highest since records began in 1996. Fighting in the Middle East has pushed energy prices up.
Food prices are rising more slowly now, by just 0.9%. The Bank of England says inflation could reach about 5% by the middle of next year.

europe.headline: Russian Missiles Land in Poland
body: Overnight, Russia attacked Ukraine with hundreds of drones and dozens of missiles. At least nine people died, and three bridges in Kyiv were damaged.
Two missiles and a drone fell in Poland, about 60 km from the border with Ukraine. Poland is a member of the EU and of NATO. Nobody in Poland was hurt.
Poland's prime minister, Donald Tusk, called it a Russian provocation. That means an action meant to stir up anger. NATO's chief, Mark Rutte, condemned it too.
